content: A multiple birth occurs when more than one fetus is carried to term during a single pregnancy. The terminology used to describe multiple births depends on the number of offspring. For example, two offspring are referred to as twins, while three are called triplets. Twins and triplets are the most common forms of multiple births, but higher-order multiples, such as quadruplets or quintuplets, also occur. Multiple births are observed across many animal species, but the term is most commonly applied to placental mammals. There are two primary types of multiple births: fraternal (dizygotic) and identical (monozygotic). Identical siblings result from the fertilization of a single egg, which subsequently splits into two or more embryos. These siblings share identical genetic material. In contrast, fraternal siblings arise when multiple eggs are fertilized and implanted, leading to genetically distinct siblings who share the same level of genetic similarity as any other full siblings. In some cases, a combination of fraternal and identical siblings can occur within a single multiple birth. For instance, a set of triplets may include one fraternal sibling and two identical twins. This phenomenon is referred to as a polyzygotic birth. A rare third type of twinning, known as polar body twinning, is hypothesized to occur when an unfertilized ovum splits into two identical cells before fertilization. Each ovum is then fertilized by a different sperm, resulting in twins who share 75% of their genetic material. These twins are sometimes called half-identical twins, but their existence has not been definitively confirmed due to the lack of DNA-based zygosity tests. The most common form of human multiple birth is twins, but higher-order multiples, such as triplets, quadruplets, and even octuplets, have been documented. The largest set of multiples in which all members survived beyond a few days was a set of septuplets born in 1997. Octuplets have also been born alive, with the first surviving set recorded in 1998. Pregnancies involving extremely high multiples, such as ten or more fetuses, have been reported, but no live births have been documented in such cases. Most of these pregnancies result from fertility treatments, although spontaneous high-order multiples have occasionally occurred. Multiple pregnancies in humans are typically delivered before the full term of 40 weeks. The average gestational length is approximately 36 weeks for twins, 34 weeks for triplets, and 32 weeks for quadruplets. The likelihood of multiple births can increase naturally due to factors such as maternal age (women over 35 are more likely to conceive multiples) or the use of fertility treatments, such as in vitro fertilization (IVF) or fertility drugs. These treatments often result in the implantation of multiple embryos or the production of multiple eggs in a single ovulatory cycle. The frequency of multiple births has increased over recent decades, largely due to the widespread use of fertility treatments. For example, in Canada, the number of multiple births rose by 35% between 1979 and 1999. Before the advent of ovulation-stimulating drugs, higher-order multiples were exceedingly rare. Today, efforts are being made to reduce the risks associated with multiple pregnancies by limiting the number of embryos transferred during IVF procedures and closely monitoring follicle production when fertility drugs are used. Multiple pregnancies carry significant risks for both the mother and the fetuses. The greater the number of fetuses, the higher the likelihood of complications such as low birth weight, premature delivery, and associated medical problems. For example, in 1999, 53% of babies from multiple births were born prematurely, compared to only 7% of singletons. There is also a higher rate of stillbirths among multiples. For mothers, virtually all obstetrical risks are increased during a multiple pregnancy. To mitigate these risks, selective reduction—a procedure in which one or more fetuses are terminated to improve the chances of a healthy outcome for the remaining fetuses—is sometimes performed. However, this procedure carries its own risks, including an increased likelihood of miscarriage for the remaining fetuses. Approximately 4-5% of women undergoing selective reduction experience a miscarriage of one or more of the remaining fetuses. The birthing process for multiples often involves a Caesarean section (C-section) rather than vaginal delivery. Multiple-birth infants are frequently admitted to neonatal intensive care units (NICUs) immediately after birth due to their increased risk of medical complications. For example, a study of triplet pregnancies found that 90% of the babies were admitted to NICUs after delivery. Cultural perceptions of multiple births vary widely. In some cultures, multiple births are seen as a blessing, while in others, they may be viewed as an omen of misfortune. For example, in Ancient Rome, the birth of identical twin boys was considered a positive sign, while identical twin girls were regarded as an unlucky burden.
